summary:
Visitors in every part of Nigeria stand under the national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 criminalises same-sex conduct nationwide and reaches beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests.

Criminal exposure attaches at entry. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (version 4.0, June 2025) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and Sharia law in all twelve states that have adopted it as criminalising same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Police violence against perceived gay people is routine. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law producing a climate of hostility independent of its text.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the SSMPA reinforced colonial-era criminalisation. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, as reported by Sahara Reporters, warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos and released on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Niger State stands under that national framework and adds a second, religious criminal track. Human Rights Watch (2004) documents the wave of Sharia adoption across the twelve states concerned, listing Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara, and tracing it from Zamfara's Shari'a Establishment Law, promulgated 27 October 1999 and in force 27 January 2000; the provisions remain in force.

Niger State's own Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000 (HB.4/2000) was signed on 22 February 2000, came into operation on 4 May 2000, and was gazetted as Niger State Gazette No. 8, Vol. 25 of 9 March 2000. It amends Penal Code Law Cap 94, Laws of Niger State, to review the punishments therein, defines 'adultery' to include sodomy, and inserts section 68A: a Muslim convicted of a listed offence and proved against him to the Islamic evidentiary standard receives the harsher Sharia-specified punishment, with amputation added to the caning paragraph of section 68, while the ordinary Penal Code punishment applies otherwise.

The state editor's note records that this is not a complete Sharia Penal Code. It amends the Penal Code of 1960 so that certain sections, applied to Muslims, carry different burdens of proof and different punishments than when applied to non-Muslims. An outed Muslim or perceived-Muslim trans visitor in Niger State therefore stands under a harsher parallel legal frame than federal law alone, and the June 2025 UK Home Office note confirms the religious layer remains in force and extends criminalisation to acts between women.
tangentialFactors:
The twelve-state Sharia bloc is a single pattern with a documented starting point: Zamfara's Shari'a Establishment Law of 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000, followed by adoption across Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara. Niger State is one instance of that bloc, not an outlier.

The UK Home Office note (June 2025) describes Nigeria's hybrid legal system, in which secular criminal law and a twelve-state religious criminal layer operate together, and notes limits in the available arrest data. Enforcement patterns are therefore documented through individual incidents rather than through reliable national statistics.

Hostility recorded against LGBTQ+ people in Nigeria is not confined to statutory charges. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs using dating apps to arrange meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing, and TimesLIVE (March 2025) records extortion and beatings by police acting on suspicion of gay appearance.

The Bobrisky case shows the state's own correctional standards being tested by trans incarceration. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations against her but found that housing a first-time offender in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act, while press coverage at sentencing openly debated which prison she should be held in.
localsOnly:
Niger State residents convicted under the Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000 face a bifurcated system. A Muslim convicted of a listed offence proved to the Islamic evidentiary standard receives the harsher punishment specified by the religious provision, including amputation where section 68 as amended provides for it; a non-Muslim, or a Muslim convicted without that standard of proof, receives the ordinary Penal Code punishment.

The amendment does not replace the Penal Code. It revises the 1960 code so that specified sections carry different burdens of proof and different penalties depending on whether the defendant is Muslim, which means residents' exposure is determined partly by religious status as recorded by the court.

Residents of the twelve states that have adopted Sharia live under a criminal layer that covers same-sex acts between women as well as between men, and that retains the death penalty for male sodomy under state Zina provisions, alongside the national SSMPA penalties of 10 to 14 years.

There is no statutory protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity for residents either; the SSMPA reinforced colonial-era criminalisation and the state amendment added a religious track rather than a protective one.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public, reported by Reuters in September 2022, have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here and should be verified against current Niger State and federal statute before publication.

The UK Home Office note (June 2025) itself records limits in the available arrest data, so the frequency with which section 68A or the SSMPA is actually charged, and against whom, remains unresolved on this inventory.

No source in this inventory documents a prosecution of a foreign visitor under Niger State's Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000; the visitor-facing risk stated here is derived from the text of the law and its applicability by religious status, not from a recorded case.

Prison placement for a trans detainee in Niger State, and whether the discretion observed in the Bobrisky case is governed by any written rule, is not sourced.
